title: NASA's Roman Telescope: A Hubble-Sized Mirror with a 100-Times Wider View
summary:
In just two days, NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will launch from Cape Canaveral, marking the arrival of the agency's next flagship astrophysics mission after the James Webb Space Telescope. Unlike Webb, which studies small regions of the universe in extraordinary depth, Roman is designed to survey vast areas of the sky quickly. Both telescopes detect infrared light, so they can work together to reveal far more than either could alone.

Roman has a 7.9-foot primary mirror—the same diameter as Hubble's—but its Wide Field Instrument can image an area 100 times larger than Hubble's cameras while matching their sensitivity. This wide view will allow Roman to find rare objects both close to Earth and across enormous cosmic distances, from dying stars to galaxy clusters.

One of Roman's main goals is to investigate dark matter and dark energy, two mysterious components that account for nearly all of the universe. Dark matter exerts gravity but doesn't emit light, while dark energy is associated with the accelerating expansion of the universe. University of Arizona researchers are leading efforts to study these phenomena. Elisabeth Krause leads a team that received $2 million to develop a technique called kinematic lensing, which combines Roman images with spectroscopic measurements to study dark matter and dark energy with greater precision than ever before.

Tim Eifler leads another group that will interpret Roman's cosmological observations. His lab received $800,000 for computing resources and $2.4 million over five years for science. "This infrastructure will take us from catalogs to cosmological interpretation," Eifler said. "We'll be able to do things like determine how much dark energy and dark matter are in the universe." He also co-chairs a cosmology group with more than 1,000 scientists worldwide.

Roman's Coronagraph Instrument will demonstrate technologies to suppress starlight, allowing astronomers to directly image exoplanets and disks around them. This is a crucial step in exoplanet science, since nearly all known exoplanets have been discovered indirectly. With Roman, we're about to see the universe in a whole new light.
why_it_matters: Roman will produce maps of the dark matter and dark energy that shape the cosmos, turning abstract physics topics into measurable data. Its survey data and exoplanet images will likely appear in textbooks and news stories for the rest of this generation's lifetime.

background_read: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is named after Nancy Grace Roman, an astronomer sometimes called the 'mother of Hubble' for her early work planning space telescopes. The James Webb Space Telescope, the current flagship that excels at peering deep into small patches of sky, works best when paired with a survey telescope like Roman; Hubble Space Telescope (the long-lived orbiting observatory that transformed astronomy) paved the way for both. Roman will launch from Cape Canaveral, the Florida site used for many historic U.S. space missions. University of Arizona researchers Elisabeth Krause and Tim Eifler are among thousands of scientists who will use Roman's data. Dark matter and dark energy are among the mission's biggest mysteries: together they govern how the universe expands and how galaxies form, but no one has directly detected either one. Roman's Wide Field Instrument and Coronagraph Instrument also continue a key quest in exoplanet science — seeing planets around other stars directly instead of inferring them from wobbles or dips in light.

perspectives.description: Roman's wide-field power lets astronomers do in years what would have taken centuries with Hubble, and its two Arizona teams show how university science connects to a flagship mission. Directly imaging exoplanets would be a historic leap in the search for other worlds.

Flagship space telescopes are enormously complex and expensive, and a single launch or instrument failure can delay progress for years. The pressure to get Roman right is high, and smaller research programs can be squeezed by the cost of supporting one massive mission.

Roman fits a recurring pattern in astronomy: each generation builds instruments that either go deeper, go wider, or both. Pairing its survey capability with Hubble and Webb's sharp eyes is a deliberate strategy to get complementary views of the universe rather than one telescope doing everything.

Once Roman starts returning data, the flood of sky surveys may reveal rare objects no one predicted and give young astronomers huge datasets to mine. Future discoveries about dark energy, exoplanet atmospheres, and galaxy evolution will be built, at least partly, on Roman's archive.
